SageMath (or just Sage) is free, open-source mathematical software built on top of Python. You might think of it as Python plus a huge number of open source libraries built in. For those familiar with Python, the basic language and idioms should seem familiar. In addition, though, there are a great many commands for performing mathematical tasks that are pre-imported into the namespsace.

## First steps with Sage

There are several ways to use Sage. By far the easiest, though, is via the [Sage Cell Server](https://sagecell.sagemath.org/){target=_blank}. If you navigate to that webpage, you'll find a code input box where you can just type code and press "Evaluate".

Even better, it's easy to embed those code boxes into any webpage. So, for example, you can press the evaluate button below to add 2 and 3:


<div class="sage">
  <script type="text/x-sage">
s = 2+3
print("2+3 =", s)
  </script>
</div>

The box is editable so that you can change it to add 3 and 4 or to solve differential equations or whatever. Here, for example, is how to solve a non-linear system of equations:

<div class="sage">
  <script type="text/x-sage">
x,y = var('x,y')
solve([x^2-3*x*y-1, y^2-3*x*y-1], [x,y])
  </script>
</div>

Now, that we see a couple of real solutions, we can plot those curves together with the solutions:

<div class="sage">
  <script type="text/x-sage">
p1 = implicit_plot(x^2 - 3*x*y - 1, (-1.6,1.6), (-1.6,1.6), fill=False)
p2 = implicit_plot(y^2 - 3*x*y - 1, (-1.6,1.6), (-1.6,1.6), fill=False)
p1+p2 + point([(-1/2,1/2), (1/2,-1/2)], size=50)  </script>
</div>

## Authoring Sage pages from notebooks

Writing longer Sage documents directly in Quarto is possible, but a Jupyter notebook is often a nicer authoring environment. The notebook `ComplexCubics.ipynb` was written that way, then converted into the live SageCell-powered page [ComplexCubics/index.qmd](ComplexCubics/index.qmd).

The converter in this directory reads a SageMath notebook, keeps the markdown cells as markdown, turns code cells into SageCell HTML blocks, and drops saved notebook outputs so the published page stays active:

```bash
./ipynb-to-sagecell-qmd.py ComplexCubics.ipynb
```

By default, the output is written to an `index.qmd` file in a folder named for the notebook. Thus, the command above writes `ComplexCubics/index.qmd`. It also copies the original notebook to `ComplexCubics/ComplexCubics.ipynb`, adds a "Notebook version" link in the right margin, and copies local files referenced by markdown cells into the same folder.

The first level-one markdown heading in the notebook becomes the Quarto page title. If you want to keep that heading in the page body too, run:

```bash
./ipynb-to-sagecell-qmd.py ComplexCubics.ipynb --keep-title-heading
```

The generated page includes the Sage Cell Server scripts automatically. If a folder eventually uses shared Quarto metadata for those scripts, use `--no-header` to leave them out of the generated document. Use `--no-copy-notebook` or `--no-notebook-link` if you want to skip those parts of the packaging.

This can also be folded into the Quarto build with a project `pre-render` script. If we do that, the cleanest long-term pattern is to keep source notebooks in an underscore-prefixed folder such as `_notebooks/`, or otherwise exclude source and copied notebooks from Quarto's render targets, so Quarto renders the generated `.qmd` pages rather than also rendering the notebooks directly.
